newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela oil spill impact seen limited.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela oil spill impact seen limited.

text.p: The environmental impact of an oil spill on Venezuela's northwestern coast appeared limited on Tuesday and a leading conservationist said he was hopeful no more oil would wash ashore.
About 11 miles (17.5 kilometres) of coastline on the western flank of the Gulf of Venezuela had been affected, but only 1-1/2 miles (2.5 kilometres) was badly harmed in Zulia state.

Along a stretch of land extending some 12 miles (20 kilometres) from the village of San Carlos to the small beach resort of Caimare Chico, white sandy beaches were fouled with black puddles, but there was no major slick.
Hundreds of men were busy scooping the oil.

"We have about 300 people cleaning the whole coast ... it's a time-consuming process, we have to be patient," said Ciro Gonzalez, local manager of environmental protection for Lagoven, a subsidiary of state oil giant Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA).

The Greek-flagged Nissos Amorgos, carrying 476,000 barrels of heavy Venezuelan crude, ran aground on Friday in a shipping channel at the mouth of Lake Maracaibo, spilling about 25,000 barrels, according to another PDVSA affiliate Maraven.
The spill grew to 60,000 barrels when the ship was moved east repairs, the Venezuelan Navy said.
Environment Minister Rafael Martinez said the environmental damage was less than initially feared. "The size of the spill is fairly smaller than what was first estimated," he told Congress.
He said he hoped the cleanup operation would be over in the worst affected area for the peak Easter holiday period.

Lenin Herrera, president of Lake Maracaibo Conservation Institute (ICLAM), an autonomous group funded by the Environment Ministry, said earlier only a tiny proportion of the 60,000 barrel spill had come ashore in Zulia.
"Up to now what we are seeing (on the coast) is nothing like the total volume of crude oil," he told Reuters.
Herrera said a strong northeasterly wind on Friday helped push the first spill away from the entrance to Lake Maracaibo out to open sea.
"If the slick had flowed into the lake it would have been an ecological disaster," he said, adding that the lake hosts a delicate ecological system with mangroves.
A spokesman for the rescue operation said late on Monday that high winds and swell hampered attempts to stem the flow of crude, but he did not know if the ship was still leaking oil on Tuesday.
The Nissos Amorgos, which was bound for Italy, is currently at anchor about 16 miles (25 km) off the west coast of Venezuela's Paraguana peninsula, in Falcon state.
